Issues.Title: Wrap DrawImageAbort in a BOOL-returning native callback
Issues.Body:
## Proposed changes

- `System.Drawing.Common` sets `[assembly: DisableRuntimeMarshalling]`, but the three `Graphics.DrawImage` overloads that take a `DrawImageAbort` pass the public delegate directly to `Marshal.GetFunctionPointerForDelegate`. `DrawImageAbort` returns `bool`, which isn't blittable.
- Since dotnet/runtime#130239, ILC builds reverse P/Invoke stubs for delegates from `DisableRuntimeMarshalling` assemblies from their managed signature. As a result, any NativeAOT app that roots these overloads gets `IL1005` on `System.Drawing.Graphics.DrawImageAbort`. Rooting can happen indirectly, for example through `DrawImage(Image, Rectangle, int, int, int, int, GraphicsUnit, ImageAttributes)`. With `IlcTreatWarningsAsErrors`, that warning becomes a build break.
- The callback now goes through a private `DrawImageAbortAdapter`, which uses a `BOOL`-returning native delegate. It mirrors the existing `EnumerateMetafileDataAdapter`. This also matches the native `ImageAbort` signature, which returns a 4-byte `BOOL`, instead of returning a 1-byte `bool`.

## Related

- ILC change that surfaced this: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/130239
- Companion fix for the same `IL1005` on `ConsoleCtrlHandlerRoutine` in `Microsoft.Win32.SystemEvents`: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/138178

## Customer Impact

- NativeAOT apps that reference `System.Drawing.Common` and use `Graphics.DrawImage` with `ImageAttributes` or a callback fail to publish when ILC warnings are treated as errors, starting with .NET 11.
- The workaround is to avoid the affected overloads or GDI+ altogether.

## Regression? 

- Yes. This is a regression with .NET 11 ILC (dotnet/runtime#130239).

## Risk

- Low. No public API changes. The change follows an existing pattern in the same type, and the null callback path still passes `0`.

## Test methodology

- No new tests. The existing test suite runs on CoreCLR, which doesn't reproduce the ILC diagnostic. The callback overloads keep their current behavior and are covered by existing `DrawImage` tests through the null-callback path.
- Found in a NativeAOT product build (`IL1005` on `DrawImageAbort`).

Issues.Title: NumericUpDown stays blank when the Minimum value is assigned after calling ResetText()
Issues.Body:
### .NET version

.NET 11.0.0.

### Did it work in .NET Framework?

Yes

### Did it work in any of the earlier releases of .NET Core or .NET 5+?

_No response_

### Issue description

When a NumericUpDown control has its **Minimum** property and **Value** property set to **1**, calling **ResetText**() through a button click correctly clears the displayed text. However, assigning **1** or **Minimum** to the **Value** property through another button click does not display the number again. The control remains blank even though its Value is still 1.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01995a54-f319-4524-a672-f9264bc031af


### Steps to reproduce

1. Add a NumericUpDown control and two buttons to a form.
2. Set the control’s Minimum and Value properties to 1.
3. Call numericUpDown1.ResetText() in the first button’s click event.
4. Set numericUpDown1.Value = numericUpDown1.Minimum in the second button’s click event.
5. Run the application and click the first button. The displayed text clears.
6. Click the second button. The control remains blank instead of displaying 1.

**Sample to reproduce the issue:** 

[NumericUpDown_Issue.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35270305/NumericUpDown_Issue.zip)

Issues.Title: Fix Issue 15482: NumericUpDown stays blank when the Minimum value is assigned after calling ResetText()
Issues.Body:
<!-- Please read CONTRIBUTING.md before submitting a pull request -->

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/issues/15482


## Proposed changes

- Restore the displayed number when the same Value is assigned after the text has been cleared.
- Preserve ResetText() behavior so it clears the display without changing the numeric value.
- Guard against recursive text restoration and add regression tests for display updates and event notifications.

## Customer Impact

• Applications can restore a cleared NumericUpDown display by assigning its current value, including Minimum.
• Existing display-clearing behavior is preserved. ValueChanged is not raised when the numeric value remains unchanged.

## Regression? 

- No

## Risk

- Low. The new restoration path applies only when the assigned value equals the current value and the displayed text is empty. Restoration raises TextChanged because the displayed text changes; a guard prevents recursive same-value restoration.

## Screenshots

### Before


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/40d54fb2-34fe-4fa1-a6a2-313b1752d54d


### After


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d9e9624b-f14f-48a5-8d4e-8f5de9ec2d22


## Test methodology

- Added unit tests to verify that ResetText() clears the display without changing the numeric value.
- Verified that assigning the same value afterward restores the displayed number and raises one TextChanged notification without raising ValueChanged.
- Covered reentrant TextChanged handlers to verify that repeated clearing and restoration do not cause an endless loop.
- Tested with and without a control handle and verified that assigning the same value preserves non-empty text.

## Accessibility testing  
     
- NA

Issues.Title: Fixes #15438
Issues.Body: Fixes #15438 ## Root Cause In Net11 mode, the button renderers rely on `ShouldSerializeBackColor()` to determine whether to use `BackColor`. After `ResetBackColor()`, that check returns false even when the effective color is inherited from the parent. Setting `BackColor` also disables `UseVisualStyleBackColor`, and that explicit opt-out remains in effect after the reset. ## Proposed changes - Make `ShouldSerializeUseVisualStyleBackColor()` available to the button renderers within the assembly. - In the Net11 color-selection paths, honor the effective `BackColor` when visual-style backgrounds have been explicitly disabled. Buttons that merely inherit a color without either setting being changed continue to use the theme color. - Add coverage for resetting an explicitly set `BackColor` on Standard, Flat and Popup buttons. ## Customer Impact - Net11 buttons, including CheckBox and RadioButton controls with `Appearance.Button`, can now display their inherited background color after `ResetBackColor()`, consistent with Classic mode for this scenario. ## Regression? - No. ## Risk - Minimal: the change is limited to the background-color decision in two renderers. The existing regression tests for dotnet/winforms#14778 continue to pass. ## Screenshots ### Before The form has a pink background. In the left column, Net11 Standard and Flat buttons remain at the neutral theme color at rest after their explicitly set backgrounds are reset; the Classic buttons on the right show the inherited pink. When clicked, Net11 buttons flash blue and Classic buttons darken slightly. These pressed-state colors are unrelated to the resting-color issue and are unchanged by this fix. ### After At rest, the Net11 buttons on the left now show the form's pink background, matching the unchanged Classic buttons on the right. Clicking still produces the same blue flash in Net11 and slight darkening in Classic as before. The Net11 pressed color comes from a separate path and uses the system accent color by design. ## Test methodology - Unit tests: the notes report three new test cases and four existing regression cases passing locally via `build.cmd -test`. The full invocation and filter were not provided. - Manual: compare the Standard and Flat buttons in the Net11 and Classic columns of the ScratchProject repro before and after the change. ## Test environment(s) - 12.0.100-alpha.1.26557.102 ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/pull/15486)

Issues.Title: Fix anchored control bounds during DPI changes
Issues.Body:
<!-- Please read CONTRIBUTING.md before submitting a pull request -->

Fixes #15477

## Root cause

During a DPI change, child controls were scaled before the form received its new bounds. Anchor information could therefore be calculated against the old display rectangle and overwritten during layout resumption.

## Proposed changes

- Apply the suggested form bounds before scaling child controls.
- Preserve scaled legacy anchor distances until layout runs.
- Add regression tests for both anchor-layout modes, nested controls, and  DPI, font, and disabled autoscaling.

<!-- We are in TELL-MODE the following section must be completed -->

## Customer Impact

- Anchored controls retain their expected position and size across DPI changes.
- Controls anchored to opposing edges no longer collapse on a DPI round trip.

- Minimal

Issues.Title: Fix issue 15458: the mouse pointer is hidden while the user moves it over menus, drop-down lists and dialogs of the form
Issues.Body:
<!-- Please read CONTRIBUTING.md before submitting a pull request -->

Fixes #15458 

## Root Cause

KioskModeManager detected mouse activity only from messages targeting the managed form or its child controls. Mouse messages for separate popup and owned windows were ignored.

When a modal dialog disabled the main form, mouse movement over the disabled form might not produce messages on the UI thread at all. As a result, the inactivity timer could hide the pointer while the user was moving it, and further movement might not restore it.

## Proposed changes

- Monitor mouse messages for windows on the same UI thread, including non-client mouse messages.
- Use a thread-specific message hook to observe messages in native modal loops and before other WinForms message filters can consume them.
- Periodically check the pointer position while fullscreen auto-hide is enabled, so movement can be detected even when no mouse message reaches the UI thread.
- Stop monitoring when auto-hide is disabled or fullscreen mode exits.
- Add regression tests for message routing, native modal loops, pointer movement, and monitoring lifecycle.

## Customer Impact

The pointer remains visible while users move it over supported popup windows, owned forms, and modal dialogs. If it has been hidden, movement over a disabled main form can restore it.

The pointer-position check also detects movement over other applications or displays, which can restore the pointer and restart the inactivity timer.

Issues.Title: Fix issue 15455: BindingContext throws duplicate-key ArgumentException when a binding manager lookup is re-entered during RelatedCurrencyManager construction
Issues.Body: Fixes #15455 ## Root Cause BindingContext.EnsureListManager checked the cache before constructing a binding manager, then used that earlier result to decide how to update the cache. Construction can synchronously invoke application code through a binding event or a property getter. If that code re-enters the lookup for the same data source and binding path, the nested call can register a manager first. When the outer call resumes, it can throw a duplicate-key ArgumentException or overwrite the manager already returned to the nested caller. ## Proposed changes - Recheck the cache after constructing a manager. If a nested lookup has already registered a live manager for the same key, return that instance instead of adding or replacing it. - Detach the discarded manager from any parent, list, or property-change events it subscribed to during construction. - Add regression tests for reentrant lookups triggered by PositionChanged on an initially empty parent list and by a child-list property getter, including a stale weak-reference cache entry. ## Customer Impact WinForms applications that initialize nested bindings from data-binding events or property getters no longer encounter the duplicate-key exception in this scenario. Existing child bindings and later lookups continue to use the same parent manager instance. No application code changes are required. ## Regression? - No ## Risk - Mini ## Screenshots ### Before ### After ## Test methodology - Manual - Automation test ## Test environment(s) - 12.0.0-alpha.1.26565.104 ## Test Project [WinForms15455Demo.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35124779/WinForms15455Demo.zip) ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/pull/15468)

The three remaining `AnchorStyles` configurations contain `Top | Left` and actually seem to work when moving to 200% DPI. However, in all three cases, when I move the Form back to the 100% DPI monitor, the width of the panel gets set to zero! * `Top | Left | Right` sets the width to zero * `Top | Left | Bottom` sets the height to zero * `Top | Left | Bottom | Right` sets both width and height to zero In all three cases, the the location seems to stay correct ### Steps to reproduce I've reduced the problem to this code sample: ```cs namespace WinFormsApp1; internal static class Program { /// /// The main entry point for the application. /// [STAThread] static void Main() { _ = Application.SetHighDpiMode(HighDpiMode.PerMonitorV2); Application.Run(new DpiTestForm()); } } class DpiTestForm : Form { private Panel panel; public DpiTestForm() { InitializeComponent(); } private void InitializeComponent() { panel = new Panel(); SuspendLayout(); // // panel // panel.Anchor = AnchorStyles.Top | AnchorStyles.Bottom; panel.Location = new Point(0, 0); panel.Size = new Size(150, 100); panel.BackColor = SystemColors.ControlDarkDark; // // Form1 // AutoScaleDimensions = new SizeF(96F, 96F); AutoScaleMode = AutoScaleMode.Dpi; ClientSize = new Size(250, 150); Controls.Add(panel); ResumeLayout(false); } } ``` And the .csproj file: ``` WinExe net10.0-windows true true ```

Issues.Title: Add HTML DOM manipulation tests for WebBrowser documents
Issues.Body:
## Proposed changes

- Add `HtmlDocumentDomManipulationTests.cs`. Existing `HtmlDocument`/`HtmlElement` tests check each API on its own; these check that the managed wrappers and the native MSHTML document stay in sync.
- Managed edits (attributes, `InnerText`, `InnerHtml`, `Style`) are visible to script in the document, and DOM changes made by script are visible through `GetElementById`/`GetElementsByTagName`.
- Lookup edge cases: duplicate ids return the first element, missing ids return null, `"*"` returns every element, id changes and `InnerHtml` replacement update lookups.
- A `CreateElement` element stays detached (no parent, not found by id) until it is appended.
- `InvokeScript` return values (string, bool, int, double, null, undefined), argument order, and a throwing script (returns null, document stays usable).
- After navigating to a new document, and after the browser is disposed (`Document` throws `ObjectDisposedException`, earlier wrappers keep working, `InvokeScript` returns null).
- Tests only, no product code changes. They use `[WinFormsFact]`/`[WinFormsTheory]` in the `Sequential` collection like the other WebBrowser tests and need no special setup.

- None; test-only change.

- No

- Minimal; test-only.

Issues.Title: Add native IDataObject interop tests for DataObject
Issues.Body:
## Proposed changes

- Add `DataObjectTests.NativeInterop.cs` with tests that call `DataObject` through its native COM `IDataObject` pointer, the way a native drag source or clipboard consumer would. Existing tests mostly go through the managed API.
- Cover `QueryGetData` (aspect, TYMED, missing format, null `FORMATETC`), `GetData`/`GetDataHere` (Unicode and ANSI text, unsupported media, null arguments, caller-allocated HGLOBAL), `GetCanonicalFormatEtc`, and `EnumFormatEtc` error paths.
- Cover native `SetData`: `E_NOTIMPL` outside a drag loop, and inside a drag loop the copy vs. ownership-transfer behavior of `fRelease`, replacing an existing value, and reading a missing format.
- Tests only, no product code changes. They use `[StaFact]`/`[StaTheory]` and need no special setup.

## Customer Impact

- None; test-only change.

## Regression?

- No

## Risk

- Minimal; test-only.

## Validation

- `.\build.cmd -configuration Debug`: succeeded, 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `System.Windows.Forms.Tests.exe --filter-method "*DataObjectTests.Native*"`: 34/34 passed, five consecutive runs.

Issues.Title: KioskModeManager: let ToggleFullScreenKeys work while focus is in a window owned by the fullscreen form
Issues.Body:
[KioskOwnedKeysRepro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35091384/KioskOwnedKeysRepro.zip)

### Background and motivation

`KioskModeManager` evaluates `ToggleFullScreenKeys` and Escape only while the managed form or one of its child controls has focus. This is documented in the `ToggleFullScreenKeys` remarks: "The key combination is evaluated only while the managed form or one of its child controls has input focus". It's implemented in [`IsMessageFromMonitoredControl`](https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/blob/f724c2277a0695ca71d1816575636afc802d73b9/src/System.Windows.Forms/System/Windows/Forms/Components/KioskModeManager/KioskModeManager.cs#L907) (`hwnd == form || IsChild(form, hwnd)`).

This matches how ordinary WinForms shortcuts behave: a `MenuStrip` shortcut of the main form doesn't run while focus is in a window owned by it either. We measured both, see below. But fullscreen isn't an ordinary command of one form:

- **It changes the window mode of the whole application surface.** While the form is fullscreen, the windows it owns are shown over it and look like part of the same fullscreen surface: tool windows, floating panels and toolbars, find/replace windows, floating documents.
- **In fullscreen, the user can't tell which window has focus.** Usually there is no caption or taskbar. After working in a floating panel, F11 silently does nothing until the user clicks the main form. To the user, the feature looks broken.
- **In "toggled fullscreen" applications (F11 like a browser or an IDE), floating windows are common.** Docking-based UIs move a large part of the application into owned windows.

For a locked kiosk, the current behavior is fine or even preferable. So we propose an opt-in option, not a change of the default.

Measured with standard controls (identical on .NET 11.0.0 and 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128; repro attached: `KioskOwnedKeysRepro.zip`):

```
1. F11 with focus in the main form: FullScreen=True (entered)
2. F11 with focus in the owned tool window: FullScreen=True (key ignored)
3. Esc with focus in the owned tool window: FullScreen=True (key ignored)
4. For comparison: the main form's menu shortcut Ctrl+N with focus in the owned tool window: ran=False
   The same shortcut with focus in the main form: ran=True
5. F11 with focus in the main form again: FullScreen=False (exited)
```

The owned tool window is created with `toolForm.Show(mainForm)`. The repro also has an interactive mode (`dotnet run`): press F11, open the tool window, click into it and press F11, Esc or Ctrl+N.

**Why this matters for third-party control libraries (DevExpress WinForms).** We develop the DevExpress WinForms controls and checked `KioskModeManager` with them (DevExpress WinForms 26.1.6, .NET 11.0.0). Applications built on `DockManager`/`DocumentManager` keep a large part of their UI in owned top-level windows: floating dock panels (`FloatForm`), floating toolbars, floating documents. F11 and Escape don't work in any of them:

```
F11 / Esc in a floating DockPanel: FullScreen=True (keys ignored; the float form is a separate top-level window)
```

A control library can't fix this from the outside:

- the component exposes no method to process a key;
- a library that calls `ToggleFullScreen()` itself would have to duplicate the key handling and the `ToggleFullScreenKeys` value, and its handling would conflict with the component's own handling in the main form.

### API Proposal

```csharp
namespace System.Windows.Forms;

public enum KioskModeKeyScope
{
    // Current behavior: the managed form and its child controls.
    Form = 0,

    // Also modeless windows owned by the managed form (owner chain), and their child controls.
    FormAndOwnedWindows = 1,
}

public partial class KioskModeManager
{
    [DefaultValue(KioskModeKeyScope.Form)]
    public KioskModeKeyScope ToggleFullScreenKeysScope { get; set; }
}
```

- **Scope.** The option applies to `ToggleFullScreenKeys` only. Escape keeps today's scope. In owned windows, Escape usually belongs to the window itself (it closes dialogs and find windows, cancels operations), so exiting fullscreen with it there would be surprising.
- **Owned windows.** A window counts as owned if its owner chain (`GetWindow(GW_OWNER)`) reaches the managed form.
- **Modal dialogs.** Windows shown with `ShowDialog` are excluded: toggling the owner's window mode behind a modal dialog is unexpected.


### API Usage

```csharp
var kiosk = new KioskModeManager
{
    ContainerControl = mainForm,
    ToggleFullScreenKeys = Keys.F11,
    ToggleFullScreenKeysScope = KioskModeKeyScope.FormAndOwnedWindows,
};

toolWindow.Show(mainForm);   // F11 in the tool window now toggles mainForm's fullscreen
```


### Alternative Designs

- **A public method that processes a key**, for example `public bool ProcessKey(Keys keyData)`, which returns `true` if the key toggled or exited fullscreen. Applications and control libraries could call it from their own owned windows (`ProcessCmdKey` of a float form). It's more flexible, but every owned window needs code.
- **Change the default** to include owned windows. This would be simpler for users, but it differs from ordinary WinForms shortcuts and from the documented behavior.
- **An application-wide scope** (any window of the UI thread). This is too broad: unrelated top-level windows would toggle the main form.

### Risks

- With the default `Form`, there is no behavior change.
- Walking the owner chain for each key-down message costs very little: it runs only for messages that match `ToggleFullScreenKeys`.
- A key that an owned window uses for its own purpose (for example, F11 in an embedded editor) would also toggle fullscreen. This is the same trade-off as in the main form today, and it's opt-in.

### Will this feature affect UI controls?

No new UI. The designer shows one new property in the Behavior category of `KioskModeManager`.

Issues.Title: KioskModeManager: a form closed in fullscreen reports the fullscreen bounds in FormClosing and is restored only after it's closed (in Dispose)
Issues.Body:
### .NET version

.NET 11.0.0 (WindowsDesktop `11.0.0+297acf930fb0f5c07fd4e51d78e521b4ad2e5d1f`). Also reproduces on .NET 11 RC 1 (`11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128`).

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, 2560×1440 at 100%, taskbar at the bottom.

### Did it work in .NET Framework?

No

### Did it work in any of the earlier releases of .NET Core or .NET 5+?

`KioskModeManager` is a new component in .NET 11.

### Issue description

### Issue description

When fullscreen is entered, the component saves the form's border style, window state, bounds and topmost state, and it restores them when fullscreen is left. But it doesn't react to the form closing. If the user closes the form while it's fullscreen (Alt+F4, a Close button, `Application.Exit`), three problems follow.

**1. The pre-fullscreen state isn't available while the form closes.** In `FormClosing`/`FormClosed`, the form reports the fullscreen state: `WindowState = Normal`, `FormBorderStyle = None`, and both `Bounds` and `RestoreBounds` equal to the screen bounds. The saved state is private, and there is no API to read it. Persisting the window layout on closing is a very common pattern. An application that uses it saves a screen-sized `Normal` window, and the next start restores a window that covers the whole screen, including the taskbar, with its caption at the very top, although fullscreen wasn't requested. For a form that was maximized before fullscreen, the "maximized" state is lost too.

`Form.RestoreBounds` exists exactly for this purpose: for a maximized or minimized form, it returns the bounds to save. For a form in kiosk fullscreen, it returns the screen bounds.

**2. The component modifies the form after it's closed.** The state is restored only in [`Dispose`](https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/blob/f724c2277a0695ca71d1816575636afc802d73b9/src/System.Windows.Forms/System/Windows/Forms/Components/KioskModeManager/KioskModeManager.cs#L566) → `ExitFullScreen`. With designer-generated code, the component sits in the form's `components` container, so it's disposed from the form's `Dispose`, after `FormClosed`. The closed form then receives `StyleChanged`, 3–4 `SizeChanged` and `Layout` events and goes through the whole restore sequence for a window that no longer exists.

**3. Code that runs on the closed form can crash.** A form that releases resources when it closes (`OnFormClosed`, `FormClosed`) and uses them in `OnStyleChanged`/`OnSizeChanged`/`OnLayout` (custom chrome, cached brushes, layout logic) throws during `Close()`. The exception comes out of `Form.Dispose` → `Container.Dispose` → `KioskModeManager.Dispose`, and the form is left not disposed (`IsDisposed = false`).

**How it works without KioskModeManager.** In `FormClosing`, `WindowState` and `RestoreBounds` describe the state the user expects to get back (for a maximized form, `RestoreBounds` holds the normal bounds). After `FormClosed`, nothing changes the form's style or size.

### Why this matters for third-party control libraries (DevExpress WinForms)

We develop the DevExpress WinForms controls and checked `KioskModeManager` with them (DevExpress WinForms 26.1.6, .NET 11.0.0).

Applications built with DevExpress commonly persist the form and layout state on closing: their own code, `WorkspaceManager` workspaces, layouts saved together with the form bounds. Closing in fullscreen persists a borderless, screen-sized `Normal` window. Measured with `RibbonForm`: before fullscreen `Normal, Sizable, {780,346, 1000x700}`; in `FormClosing` `Bounds={0,0,2560x1440}, RestoreBounds={0,0,2560x1440}, WindowState=Normal, Border=None`. DevExpress `RibbonControl` has its own fullscreen mode, and it keeps the pre-fullscreen state for exactly this reason. `KioskModeManager` exposes nothing similar.

### Suggested fix

1. Make the pre-fullscreen state available while the form closes:
   - while the form is in kiosk fullscreen, have `Form.RestoreBounds` return the saved bounds, just as it does for a maximized form; and/or
   - expose the saved state on the component (for example, read-only `RestoreBounds`, `RestoreWindowState`, `RestoreFormBorderStyle`).
2. Don't modify a form that is closing or closed. Handle `FormClosed`/`HandleDestroyed` of the target form: stop fullscreen without applying the saved state to the window, release the target, and make `Dispose` a no-op for a closed form.
3. Optionally, restore the state *before* `FormClosing` is raised (for example, on `WM_CLOSE`) without visible transitions. Today, exiting fullscreen on closing causes 4 visible window resizes (see the workaround).

### Steps to reproduce

Minimal repro project (attached: `KioskClosingRepro.zip`, a single `Program.cs`). It uses a designer-style form: `KioskModeManager` is created in the form's `components` container, and `Dispose` calls `components.Dispose()`.

```csharp
// Typical "persist the window layout" code
form.FormClosing += (_, _) =>
{
    Settings.Bounds = form.WindowState == FormWindowState.Normal ? form.Bounds : form.RestoreBounds;
    Settings.WindowState = form.WindowState;
};

// Designer-style form
readonly IContainer components = new Container();
KioskModeManager kiosk = new(components) { ContainerControl = this };   // F11 toggles
protected override void Dispose(bool disposing)
{
    if (disposing) components.Dispose();
    base.Dispose(disposing);
}
```

1. Run the app (`dotnet run`). Press **F11**, then close the form with **Alt+F4**.
2. The app opens a second form and applies the settings saved in `FormClosing`. It covers the whole screen.

`dotnet run -- --auto` runs these cases and writes `results.txt`:

1. normal form → fullscreen → close;
2. maximized form → fullscreen → close;
3. restoring the saved settings on the next start;
4. the workaround described below;
5. a form that releases a resource in `OnFormClosed` and uses it in `OnStyleChanged`.

**Expected:**

- in `FormClosing`, the application can get the pre-fullscreen state (for example, `RestoreBounds`/`WindowState` describe it, or the component exposes it);
- nothing modifies the form after `FormClosed`;
- closing a form in fullscreen never throws.

**Actual:** (identical on .NET 11.0.0 and 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128)

```
1. Normal form -> fullscreen -> closed
  before fullscreen: WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=880,Y=396,Width=800,Height=600}
  in FormClosing:    WindowState=Normal, Border=None, Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, RestoreBounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}
  saved settings:    Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, WindowState=Normal
  events on the CLOSED form (KioskModeManager.Dispose via the form's components):
    [Layout, SizeChanged(Normal, 2560x1440), StyleChanged(Border=Sizable), Layout, SizeChanged(Normal, 2576x1460), Layout, SizeChanged(Normal, 800x600)]

2. Maximized form -> fullscreen -> closed
  before fullscreen: WindowState=Maximized, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=-8,Y=-8,Width=2576,Height=1408}, RestoreBounds={X=880,Y=396,Width=800,Height=600}
  in FormClosing:    WindowState=Normal, Border=None, Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, RestoreBounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}
  saved settings:    Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, WindowState=Normal          <- "maximized" is lost as well
  events on the CLOSED form: [..., SizeChanged(Normal, 800x600), Layout, SizeChanged(Maximized, 2576x1408)]

3. Next start restores the settings saved in case 1 (no fullscreen requested)
  restored window: WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, kiosk.FullScreen=False
  covers the screen including the taskbar area: True

5. Form that releases a resource in OnFormClosed and uses it in OnStyleChanged
  NullReferenceException: ResourceForm.OnStyleChanged <- Form.UpdateFormStyles <- Form.set_FormBorderStyle
    <- KioskModeManager.ExitFullScreen <- KioskModeManager.Dispose <- Component.Dispose <- Container.Dispose
  form IsDisposed=False
```

Issues.Title: KioskModeManager: pointer auto-hide uses the shared ShowCursor counter and conflicts with the application's own Cursor.Hide/Cursor.Show
Issues.Body:
### .NET version

.NET 11.0.0 (WindowsDesktop `11.0.0+297acf930fb0f5c07fd4e51d78e521b4ad2e5d1f`). Also reproduces on .NET 11 RC 1 (`11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128`).

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200.

### Did it work in .NET Framework?

No

### Did it work in any of the earlier releases of .NET Core or .NET 5+?

`KioskModeManager` is a new component in .NET 11.

### Issue description

With `MousePointerAutoHideDelay` set, the component hides and shows the pointer with `Cursor.Hide()`/`Cursor.Show()` ([`OnMousePointerAutoHideTimerTick`](https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/blob/f724c2277a0695ca71d1816575636afc802d73b9/src/System.Windows.Forms/System/Windows/Forms/Components/KioskModeManager/KioskModeManager.cs#L798), [`ShowMousePointerIfHidden`](https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/blob/f724c2277a0695ca71d1816575636afc802d73b9/src/System.Windows.Forms/System/Windows/Forms/Components/KioskModeManager/KioskModeManager.cs#L834)). These are `ShowCursor(FALSE/TRUE)`: they change the display counter shared by all code on the UI thread. The pointer is visible while the counter is >= 0.

The component keeps its own calls balanced, as the API review requires: "Cursor hiding must remain balanced because Cursor.Hide/Cursor.Show affect an internal display counter" (#14586). But the application's calls go to the same counter. An application that hides the pointer itself, for example a video player during playback, a presentation mode, or a drawing tool, gets results that depend on what the component did before:

- **A. The application's `Cursor.Hide()` stops working.** The application shows the pointer while the component has it hidden (for example, a dialog needs the pointer). Then, when the mouse moves, the component balances its own hide with `Cursor.Show()`. The counter is now one higher than the application expects. Its next `Cursor.Hide()` leaves the pointer visible, and every later `Hide`/`Show` pair of the application stays shifted by one for the rest of the session.
- **B. The application's `Cursor.Show()` doesn't show the pointer.** The application hides the pointer (playback started). While it's hidden, the component also hides it after the delay. When the application shows the pointer (playback paused), the counter is still negative because of the component's hide. The pointer appears only after the user moves the mouse.

The counter also applies to every window of the UI thread, not only to the kiosk form. While the component has the pointer hidden, it's hidden over all the application's windows.

**How it works without KioskModeManager.** Each piece of code that calls `Cursor.Hide()` balances it with its own `Cursor.Show()`. Pointer shapes are normally changed with `Cursor.Current`/`WM_SETCURSOR`, which doesn't touch the counter. A component that hides the pointer *on its own schedule* (a timer and mouse activity) breaks the assumption that only one party uses the counter at a time.

### Why this matters for third-party control libraries (DevExpress WinForms)

We develop the DevExpress WinForms controls and checked `KioskModeManager` with them (DevExpress WinForms 26.1.6, .NET 11.0.0). DevExpress controls change pointer *shapes* with `Cursor.Current`, which is unaffected. But, like other control libraries, they also call `Cursor.Hide()`/`Cursor.Show()` in balanced pairs for specific interactions:

- the color picker magnifier (`ColorPickEdit` → `MagnifierForm`) hides the pointer when the magnifier opens and shows it when it closes;
- `GanttControl` hides the pointer while the user drags a task's progress handle;
- menus and popups hide it for a moment while they draw.

Pairs that span a user interaction can interleave with the component's own hide/show. For example, the magnifier is a separate top-level window, and the component doesn't count mouse movement over it (see the separate issue about owned windows). So the component hides the pointer while the magnifier is open as well. When the magnifier closes, its `Cursor.Show()` leaves the pointer hidden until the user moves the mouse back over the form (case B). This example follows from the code and the measurements above; we didn't measure it separately with DevExpress.

The library can't avoid this: the counter is shared by design, and there is no way to know whether `KioskModeManager` currently holds a hide.

### Suggested fix

Hide the pointer without the shared counter. For example, while the pointer should be hidden, handle `WM_SETCURSOR` for the kiosk form and its windows, and call `SetCursor(NULL)` (return `TRUE`). When the pointer should be visible again, stop doing it and send a `WM_SETCURSOR` refresh. This:

- doesn't interfere with the application's `Cursor.Hide()`/`Cursor.Show()`;
- limits the hiding to the kiosk form instead of every window of the thread;
- needs no balancing in `Dispose`/`ExitFullScreen`.


### Steps to reproduce

Minimal repro project (attached: `KioskCursorCounterRepro.zip`, a single `Program.cs`). It contains a form with `KioskModeManager { MousePointerAutoHideDelay = 2000 }` and two buttons that call `Cursor.Hide()`/`Cursor.Show()` (the application's own pointer hiding). The status line shows the display counter.

```csharp
KioskModeManager kiosk = new() { ContainerControl = form, MousePointerAutoHideDelay = 2000 };   // F11 toggles

Button appHide = new() { Text = "App: Cursor.Hide()  (e.g. playback started)" };
appHide.Click += (_, _) => Cursor.Hide();
Button appShow = new() { Text = "App: Cursor.Show()  (e.g. playback paused)" };
appShow.Click += (_, _) => Cursor.Show();
```

Use Tab and Space to press the buttons, so that the mouse doesn't move unless a step says so.

Case A:

1. Press **F11**. Don't touch the mouse until the component hides the pointer.
2. Press **App: Cursor.Show()**. The pointer appears.
3. Move the mouse a little.
4. Press **App: Cursor.Hide()**.

**Expected:** the pointer is hidden. **Actual:** the pointer stays visible.

Case B:

1. Press **App: Cursor.Hide()**. Move the mouse, then leave it still until the delay passes.
2. Press **App: Cursor.Show()**.

**Expected:** the pointer is visible. **Actual:** it stays hidden until the mouse is moved.

`dotnet run -- --auto` runs both cases (`MousePointerAutoHideDelay = 500`) and writes `results.txt`. The probe that reads the counter never crosses the visibility threshold: crossing it makes Windows send a synthetic `WM_MOUSEMOVE`, which the component would treat as user activity.

Measured (identical on .NET 11.0.0 and 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128; the values are the display counter, >= 0 means visible):

```
A. The application's Cursor.Hide() stops working
   start: 0 -> component hid the pointer after the delay: -1 -> app Cursor.Show() (e.g. a dialog needs the pointer): 0
   -> mouse moved (component calls Cursor.Show()): 1 -> app Cursor.Hide(): 0 -> later: app Cursor.Show() + Cursor.Hide() pair: 0
   Result: after the app's Cursor.Hide() the pointer is VISIBLE (expected: hidden). The counter stays shifted by +1.

B. The application's Cursor.Show() doesn't show the pointer
   start: 0 -> app Cursor.Hide() (playback started): -1 -> mouse moved: -1 -> component hid the pointer after the delay: -2
   -> app Cursor.Show() (playback paused): -1 -> mouse moved (component calls Cursor.Show()): 0
   Result: after the app's Cursor.Show() the pointer is HIDDEN (expected: visible); it appears only after the mouse moves.
```

Issues.Title: KioskModeManager: re-parenting the ContainerControl silently moves fullscreen to another form (including MDI child forms)
Issues.Body:
### .NET version

.NET 11.0.0 (WindowsDesktop `11.0.0+297acf930fb0f5c07fd4e51d78e521b4ad2e5d1f`). Also reproduces on .NET 11 RC 1 (`11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128`).

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, 2560×1440 at 100%.

### Did it work in .NET Framework?

No

### Did it work in any of the earlier releases of .NET Core or .NET 5+?

`KioskModeManager` is a new component in .NET 11.

### Issue description

`ContainerControl` intentionally accepts a `UserControl`. From the property remarks: "A KioskModeManager can be placed on a UserControl at design time, and that user control can later be hosted by a form." The component then targets the form that hosts the user control. It subscribes to `ParentChanged` of the whole parent chain, and [`OnContainerControlParentChanged`](https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/blob/f724c2277a0695ca71d1816575636afc802d73b9/src/System.Windows.Forms/System/Windows/Forms/Components/KioskModeManager/KioskModeManager.cs#L647) re-applies fullscreen to the new form. Following the hosting form is by design. However, the way it happens causes three problems.

**1. Fullscreen silently moves to another form.** When the user control is moved to another top-level form (for example, a docking framework floats a document), the original form leaves fullscreen and the new form becomes fullscreen. The application gets no chance to decide. The component raises `FullScreenChanged` as `False, True`, while `FullScreen` stays `true` before and after. A handler can't tell that the kiosk surface moved to another window. In a locked kiosk, this is the worst case: the main kiosk form silently becomes a normal, movable window again.

**2. Removing the control and adding it back to the same form exits and re-enters fullscreen.** A control is often removed and added back within one operation: view switching, layout reloading, docking frameworks re-docking a panel. Each time, the form is restored to its normal bounds and then made fullscreen again, so the user sees two full transitions. While the control is detached, `FullScreen` returns `true` (the request is pending), but no window is fullscreen.

**3. An MDI child form (or any non-top-level form) becomes the target.** If the user control ends up in an MDI child, `FindForm()` returns the MDI child, and the component applies fullscreen to it:

- the child gets `FormBorderStyle = None` and the screen bounds (2560×1440) *inside the MDI client area* (863×590), so it's clipped and offset;
- the main form leaves fullscreen;
- `FullScreen` stays `true`, although no window covers the screen.

The screen is also computed from the child's client-relative bounds (`Screen.FromRectangle`), so the size of the primary monitor is used even when the MDI parent is on another monitor.

**How it works without KioskModeManager.** Moving a user control between forms or containers changes nothing about the window state of any form.

### Why this matters for third-party control libraries (DevExpress WinForms)

We develop the DevExpress WinForms controls and checked `KioskModeManager` with them (DevExpress WinForms 26.1.6, .NET 11.0.0). Re-parenting user controls is the core of docking and document-management frameworks:

- `DocumentManager` floats a document into its own form, docks it back, and moves documents between Tabbed, Widget and native MDI views. The native MDI view hosts documents in MDI child forms (case 3).
- `DockManager` floats panels into separate float forms and docks them back.
- Applications built on these frameworks commonly put each screen into a `UserControl` shown as a document. This is exactly the `UserControl` scenario `ContainerControl` is designed for.

With a `KioskModeManager` placed on such a user control, floating the document makes the floating document form fullscreen and restores the main form. A kiosk application expects the opposite. Measured with DevExpress (`DocumentManager` + `TabbedView`, `ContainerControl` = the document's `XtraUserControl`):

```
main form after F11:                     Normal, Border=None,    {0,0, 2560x1440}, FullScreen=True
main form after Controller.Float(doc):   Normal, Border=Sizable, {780,346, 1000x700}   (restored)
floating document form:                  Normal, Border=None,    {3,26, 2560x1440}, FullScreen=True, events=[True, False, True]
```

The floating document form isn't even placed at the screen origin. It's shifted by (3, 26) px, and its right and bottom parts are off-screen.

A control library can't prevent this:

- there is no event before the target form changes;
- the component reacts to `ParentChanged` synchronously, inside the framework's own re-parenting code;
- after the fact, `FullScreenChanged` with an unchanged `FullScreen` value doesn't say which form is now fullscreen.

### Suggested fix

1. **Never target a non-top-level form.** Resolve the target to the top-level form (for an MDI child, its `MdiParent`), or ignore the change if the new form isn't top-level.
2. **Coalesce re-parenting.** Defer the re-targeting decision until the parent change settles (for example, `BeginInvoke`), and do nothing if the resolved form is the same as before. This removes the exit/enter pair in case 2.
3. **Let the application control re-targeting.** Raise an event before fullscreen moves to another form, for example `TargetFormChanging` with the old and new form and `Cancel`. Alternatively, add an option to stay on the original form or to exit fullscreen when the target form changes. Expose the current target form, for example a read-only `TargetForm` property, so a handler can see which window the component controls.
4. Don't report `FullScreen == true` while no form is fullscreen, or document the pending state clearly.

### Steps to reproduce

Minimal repro project (attached: `KioskReparentRepro.zip`, a single `Program.cs`). It contains a main form with a `UserControl` host, `KioskModeManager.ContainerControl = host` (default settings), and three buttons.

```csharp
UserControl host = new() { Dock = DockStyle.Fill };
form.Controls.Add(host);
KioskModeManager kiosk = new() { ContainerControl = host };   // the documented UserControl scenario
kiosk.FullScreenChanged += (_, _) => Log($"FullScreenChanged {kiosk.FullScreen}");

// 1. Move to another form
Form other = new() { Text = "Other form" };
other.Show();
other.Controls.Add(host);

// 2. Remove and add back
form.Controls.Remove(host);
form.Controls.Add(host);

// 3. Move into an MDI child
Form mdiParent = new() { IsMdiContainer = true };
Form mdiChild = new() { MdiParent = mdiParent };
mdiParent.Show(); mdiChild.Show();
mdiChild.Controls.Add(host);
```

1. Run the app (`dotnet run`) and press **F11**. The main form is fullscreen.
2. Click **1. Move the host to another form**, **2. Remove the host and add it back**, or **3. Move the host into an MDI child form**. Start each case from fullscreen on the main form.

`dotnet run -- --auto` runs all three cases and writes `results.txt`.

**Expected:**

1. Fullscreen doesn't move to another window without the application's consent. Either it stays on the original form or exits, or the application is asked first. Any change of the target form is reported in a way a handler can detect.
2. Removing the control and adding it back to the same form doesn't change the window state.
3. A non-top-level form (MDI child, `TopLevel = false`) is never made fullscreen.

**Actual:** (identical on .NET 11.0.0 and 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128)

```
1. Move the host UserControl to another top-level form
  main form after kiosk.FullScreen = true: WindowState=Normal, Border=None, Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}
  after otherForm.Controls.Add(host):
    main form:  WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=880,Y=396,Width=800,Height=600}      <- left fullscreen
    other form: WindowState=Normal, Border=None,    Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}       <- became fullscreen
    kiosk.FullScreen=True, FullScreenChanged sequence=[False, True]

2. Remove the host from the form and add it back to the same form
  while the host is removed:
    main form:  WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=880,Y=396,Width=800,Height=600}      <- restored
    kiosk.FullScreen=True, FullScreenChanged sequence=[False]                                         <- FullScreen=True, nothing is fullscreen
  after the host is added back:
    main form:  WindowState=Normal, Border=None,    Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}        <- fullscreen again
    kiosk.FullScreen=True, FullScreenChanged sequence=[False, True]

3. Move the host into an MDI child form
  after mdiChild.Controls.Add(host):
    main form:  WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=880,Y=396,Width=800,Height=600}      <- left fullscreen
    MDI parent: WindowState=Normal, Border=Sizable, Bounds={X=50,Y=50,Width=900,Height=650}
    MDI child:  WindowState=Normal, Border=None,    Bounds={X=0,Y=0,Width=2560,Height=1440}, TopLevel=False, IsMdiChild=True
    MDI client area on screen: {X=60,Y=83,Width=863,Height=590}                                      <- the "fullscreen" child is clipped by it
    kiosk.FullScreen=True, FullScreenChanged sequence=[False, True]
```
